author: Basil of Caesarea
occasion: Basil preaches to a large assembly at Lakizoi, urging them to profit from the morning's scriptural readings and to apply each text as a remedy for their particular sins.
argument: Basil opens by urging the congregation to resist distraction and gather spiritual profit from the morning readings, since each person's passions require a matching remedy. He expounds the proverb 'He who sees smooth things will be shown mercy' as a call to impartiality toward rich and poor, friend and stranger. He then treats anger, envy, and greed as destructive passions, showing how each Scripture passage supplies its own cure. Envy is traced to the devil, who envied humanity's honor and still attacks God through God's image in human beings. Basil closes by interpreting the man who fell among robbers as a figure of the soul wounded by sin and stripped of grace, and he exhorts his hearers to return home renewed.

outline.move: Basil urges the congregation to attend to the morning's readings and to take from them the remedy suited to each person's passion.
He expounds 'He who sees smooth things will be shown mercy' as a command to treat rich and poor, friend and stranger alike.
He applies the proverb to anger, describing how the angry man loses human dignity and becomes like a beast.
He turns to greed, warning that the land remains behind while sin follows the soul, and that greed consumes the greedy man with anxiety.
He warns against using children as an excuse for greed and urges parents to leave their children a good name rather than ill-gotten wealth.
He returns to envy, explaining that it is the devil's own passion, and recounts the devil's fall and the detailed creation narrative showing why the devil envied humanity's honor.

He describes how the devil had no handle on humanity until the woman was created, turned her natural gentleness toward vice, and still blocks the return to paradise through envy and deceit; he exhorts his hearers to remember their noble origin and exile.

He uses the analogy of a leopard attacking a drawn image to show that the devil attacks God's image in humanity because he cannot attack God directly, and interprets the man going down from Jerusalem to Jericho as the soul wounded by sin and stripped of grace.

key_terms.sense: smooth, level; figuratively, impartial and even-handed treatment of persons
uneven, rough; figuratively, partiality and favoritism
envy, the begrudging of another's prosperity
one who greedily takes more, especially by seizing another's land or property
greed, the drive to acquire more than one's due
wound or blow; figuratively, each sin that wounds the soul
stripping; figuratively, the loss of the garment of incorruption through sin
restoration, the return to paradise and original blessedness
regeneration, the baptismal washing that grants grace

scripture: Basil quotes Proverbs in the Septuagint form and alludes to the parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:30). Psalm numbering follows the Septuagint. Modern citations should use standard English Bible book names and, where applicable, note Septuagint numbering.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἐκεῖνος κατήγαγεν ἀπὸ Ἱερουσαλὴμ εἰς Ἱεριχὼ τὸν ἄνθρωπον, ἀπὸ τῶν ὑψηλῶν ἐπὶ τὰ κοῖλα... Ἀπὸ τοίνυν τῶν ὑψηλῶν ἐπὶ τὰ κάτω ἦλθεν ὁ ἄνθρωπος, ἵνα τοῖς λῃσταῖς περιπέσῃ
_unresolved_facts.fix: the man: 'humanity/the human being' (ὁ ἄνθρωπος) — Basil uses the singular 'man' as a figure for humanity in general, not specifically 'the soul'; the descent from Jerusalem to Jericho represents humanity's fall, with the robbers being demons and sins

_unresolved_facts.fix: The source explicitly states the devil had no 'handle' (λαβήν) on humanity until the woman was created, but this is presented as the devil's opportunity, not that the woman herself was the cause; the brief's wording is accurate but should note the nuance that the devil exploited her 'gentleness' (ἁπαλότητα)

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἐπὶ πᾶσιν οἱονεὶ κορωνίδα ἐπίθετε τῶν εὐαγγελικῶν ῥημάτων τὴν μνήμην
_unresolved_facts.fix: Scripture voices include: Proverbs (quoted with ὅτι and direct quotation in sections 1-5), but also Psalm references (section 1: 'τὰ ψαλμικὰ διδάγματα'), apostolic exhortations (section 1), and Gospel/Evangelical words (section 1, 5, 8); the brief omits that section 6 quotes 'Μὴ συνδείπνει ἀνδρὶ βασκάνῳ' which was already cited in section 3, and section 8 alludes to Luke 10:30 without direct quotation marks

The names are present but the brief omits that Basil explicitly notes the geographical details: Jerusalem is on the mountain heights (ἐπὶ τῆς κορυφῆς), Jericho is in the lowlands near the Dead Sea (ἐν τῇ ἁλμυρᾷ θαλάσσῃ, κοῖλα τῆς Παλαιστίνης), and he appeals to eyewitness knowledge of the terrain
